scope: Mechanical sentence/paragraph and numeric checks, not full STE dictionary or translation validation

sentence_audit.text: Space networks do not always provide a continuous path from a source node to a destination node.
Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN) supports data transfer across these periods without a continuous path.
Nodes keep data until a contact becomes available.
In this study, a bundle is the unit of data that the routing method must transfer.
Each contact has a sender, a receiver, a time window, a data rate, and a propagation delay.
A Contact Plan describes these contacts.
The study treats each bundle as a whole unit.
The method cannot divide a bundle between contacts on the same hop.
A node must receive the complete bundle before it can send the bundle to the next node.
Each node has a buffer limit.
Earlier bundles can use contact time and buffer space that a later bundle also needs.
Thus, the method must use the current resource reservations when it plans a route.
Enough total contact capacity does not mean that a continuous transmission slot is available.
A contact can contain a free slot that starts after an occupied slot.
The method must find a slot long enough to send the complete bundle.
Enough buffer space at full arrival does not prove that reception is feasible.
The buffer limit must hold throughout reception.
The same limit must hold while the node keeps or sends the bundle.
An early arrival can require a wait through a period with insufficient buffer space.
A later arrival can avoid that period.
Thus, arrival time alone does not show that one label can replace another label.
Earlier drafts tested transmission start times on a time grid.
The current candidate uses feasible start intervals instead.
This change removes the need to create a label for each time-grid point.
The literature review found strong overlap with an existing study.
That study uses contact splitting, buffer forecasts, and contact-sequence restrictions.
It also plans bundles one at a time and updates resource reservations.
These features cannot support a claim that this study introduces a new method.
The research must identify a specific difference and test that difference.
One candidate difference concerns the cost of resource calculations.
The main objective is to find the earliest feasible arrival for each bundle under existing resource reservations.
The output must include the route and the transmission start time on each contact.
First, the study will define consistent time, contact capacity, and buffer constraints.
These definitions must distinguish contact availability from the buffer space that a receiver needs.
Second, the study will determine feasible start intervals without time-grid enumeration.
Each interval must satisfy the contact window and the applicable resource limits.
Third, the study will test whether the search retains all necessary route candidates.
A complete route must satisfy the buffer limit during reception, storage, and transmission.
The method must distinguish an incomplete search from a search that proves no feasible route exists.
Fourth, the study will compare methods under the same model and input data.
The comparison will include arrival time, calculation time, memory use, and failure cases.
An additional candidate objective is to reduce repeated resource calculations.
The candidate calculates intervals on demand and reuses valid results.
The study has not established this candidate as a new research contribution.
The project has a candidate label definition and route-search flow.
Fixed route examples support the explanations in the current presentation.
The complete candidate search does not yet have a verified implementation.
The project has a separate interval component for continuous buffer curves.
Nine analytical cases matched their expected interval results.
The tests found no differences across 9,307 fixed-start comparisons and 22,320 cache-answer comparisons.
These checks do not prove that the complete route search is correct.
The component experiment used 96 contacts and five resource snapshots.
Each strategy had seven timed runs.
For the local-update case with 10% contact queries, the on-demand median was 28.443 milliseconds.
The full incremental strategy required 228.056 milliseconds.
Both values represent the total time across five snapshots.
When queries covered all contacts, the on-demand strategy had no consistent time advantage.
These results support only a conditional component benefit.
The experiment did not compare the candidate with the published algorithm.
The current route model plans one bundle at a time in a fixed order.
The model assumes known contacts and resource reservations.
The model does not optimize all bundles together.
The component experiment excludes predecessor waiting, occupancy jumps, and full-route resource updates.
The experiment also excludes random contact failures and shared-radio constraints.
Thus, the results do not establish operational performance or complete-search optimality.
The research contribution remains unconfirmed.
The next validation step is to measure resource queries during a complete search.
That measurement must determine whether on-demand calculation reduces total route-planning time.
